I need to write JUnit 4 tests for Joda-Time's PeriodFormatterBuilder, covering most of the public API like appendLiteral, appendPrefix, appendSuffix, the appendSeparator variants, printZero methods, minimumPrintedDigits, maximumParsedDigits, rejectSignedValues, the toFormatter/toPrinter/toParser conversions, append with formatter or printer/parser pairs, and clear.

I also need to cover the field append methods for years, months, weeks, days, hours, minutes, seconds, secondsWithMillis, secondsWithOptionalMillis, millis, and millis3Digit, along with exception cases: null text throwing IllegalArgumentException, calling appendSuffix before appending a field throwing IllegalStateException, consecutive separators throwing IllegalStateException, calling toFormatter on an empty builder throwing IllegalStateException, and append(null) or append(null,null) throwing IllegalArgumentException. I want the tests to exercise real printing and parsing with Period and PeriodType objects to actually catch the known Defects4J Time-27 fault, which I believe relates to appendSeparator behavior, though I'm not certain of the exact root cause so I should aim to cover as many branches as possible.

I'm planning out specific test methods: verifying that clear() resets builder state (checking that printing after clear produces an empty string since no elements exist), confirming appendLiteral(null) throws IllegalArgumentException, checking that appendLiteral("X") followed by toFormatter() prints "X" for any period, and testing that appending null formatters or null printer/parser pairs both throw IllegalArgumentException.

Beyond that I want to cover cases where only a printer or only a parser is appended (ensuring toParser or toPrinter returns null appropriately), null prefix handling, appendPrefix combined with a field producing something like "P5", and appendSuffix throwing IllegalStateException when called without a preceding field or after a non-field element like a literal.

I also need singular/plural suffix tests comparing output for value 1 versus 2, null exception checks for the two-arg appendPrefix, minimum printed digits formatting (e.g. "005"), maximum parsed digits and rejecting signed values during parsing, and the various printZero settings (always, never, rarely-first, rarely-last, if-supported) verified against periods containing zero values.

Then for appendSeparator I'm checking basic usage -- days and hours joined by a comma, confirming the separator appears when both fields print and disappears when only one does, which requires careful period type setup or forcing printZeroAlways. I also need to cover the conditional separator variants (if-fields-after/before) and the case of two adjacent separator calls with nothing between them, which should throw an IllegalStateException since there's no field pair to separate.

Looking more carefully at the logic, calling appendSeparator as the very first call with default useBefore/useAfter is actually a harmless no-op since pairs.size()==0 doesn't trigger the append condition, whereas appendSeparatorIfFieldsAfter does append in that same situation since its useBefore is false. So the behavior differs based on which separator variant is called first, which is worth testing explicitly.

Then if a second separator call follows right after one that already appended, it should throw an IllegalStateException for adjacent separators -- I want a test case verifying that, plus a case checking the finalText variant behaves correctly when the separator is or isn't the last one in the chain.

I should also cover appendSeconds with optional millis printing, three-digit millis formatting, and the edge case of appending a printer/parser pair where the printer is null -- checking that toPrinter() returns null and printing in that state likely throws an NPE.

For testing toFormatter() with neither printer nor parser present, I'm reasoning through whether that's even reachable: append0 only fires when at least one of printer/parser is non-null, so the only way to get an empty state is a completely fresh builder with no appends at all.

A fresh builder has both flags false by default, so toFormatter() on it actually succeeds, producing an empty literal formatter that prints "" and parses nothing. To force the exception, I'd need both iNotPrinter and iNotParser true simultaneously, which would require appending something printer-only followed by something parser-only.

I can get a usable PeriodPrinter/PeriodParser pair by building a simple literal formatter elsewhere and extracting its printer and parser via the public accessor methods, then feeding those into the two append calls to trigger the combined flag state.

This confirms the append call passes validation and sets the internal flags correctly, giving me what I need to test the toFormatter() exception path.

Next I want to test isSupported behavior with PRINT_ZERO_ALWAYS on a field type that the PeriodType doesn't actually support—it should still print since the type check gets bypassed when ALWAYS is set.

I also need to verify how get() behaves on an unsupported duration field type for a given period type—I recall Joda's AbstractPeriod.get just returns 0 rather than throwing, so I shouldn't worry too much about exceptions there.

Then I want to test rejectSignedValues with a negative value like "-5" to confirm the parser correctly fails and throws IllegalArgumentException.

I should also check maximumParsedDigits for limiting how many digits get consumed during parsing.

Another case worth testing is chaining appendPrefix twice before a field—this should merge into a CompositeAffix, so calling appendPrefix("A").appendPrefix("B").appendYears() should print "AB5" for a value of 5.

Similarly, I want to verify that calling appendSuffix twice in a row after a field also composes correctly, so appendYears().appendSuffix("Y1").appendSuffix("Y2") should combine into "Y1Y2" via the CompositeAffix logic in FieldFormatter.

I also want to check whether clearPrefix() throws an IllegalStateException if a prefix is set but not followed by a field—I need to trace through whether appendSuffix validates the prefix state before proceeding.

So clearPrefix detects the orphaned iPrefix and throws "Prefix not followed by field" - testing appendYears().appendPrefix("X").appendSuffix("S") should trigger exactly that exception. I also need to verify appendLiteral triggers the same clearPrefix check.

Extending this pattern, I should also confirm append(formatter), append(printer,parser), and appendSeparator all invoke clearPrefix() and throw similarly when a prefix is set without a field. I want to also hit the PRINT_ZERO_RARELY_LAST/FIRST branches in FieldFormatter with multiple fields to check output switching behavior, aiming for a solid but not exhaustive set of roughly 30-40 targeted test methods, and I still need to decide on concrete Period/PeriodType objects to use.

I'm figuring out the simplest way to construct a Period with specific values for years, months, weeks, days, hours, minutes, seconds, and millis, settling on using Period.ZERO and chaining the withXxx methods rather than wrestling with constructor overloads.

For testing an unsupported field scenario, I'm considering creating a custom PeriodType that excludes months, possibly using something like PeriodType.standard().withMonthsRemoved() if that method exists.

I'm confirming the full constructor signature for Period that takes all eight fields plus a custom PeriodType, which should let me build test periods with specific unsupported fields.

PeriodFormatter also has print() and parsePeriod() methods I'll need for round-trip testing. Now I'm thinking through the printZeroRarelyLast/First branch logic carefully so my expected test outputs match actual source behavior rather than assumptions.

So the "last" in RARELY_LAST actually means preferring the zero to appear on the latest field when all are zero -- if a later supported field exists, this one suppresses and defers to it; otherwise it prints zero here. PRINT_ZERO_RARELY_FIRST works the same way but checks earlier fields instead.

For PRINT_ZERO_IF_SUPPORTED, there's no special case in the switch -- it just falls through and returns the zero value as long as the field is supported (unsupported fields already got filtered out earlier). PRINT_ZERO_ALWAYS skips this check entirely since it never reaches the zero-value branch.

Now I'm working through RARELY_LAST with multiple zero fields, tracing how the suppression loop decides which field gets to print the zero value. For a years-zero/months-zero period, years checks ahead to months (supported and registered) and defers by returning MAX_VALUE, while months checks whether it's the designated "last" zero field by scanning further ahead through the remaining field types.

Since no formatters exist past months, nothing supersedes it, so months ends up printing "0" while years is fully suppressed, including skipping its printed length so it contributes nothing to output. I'm now also considering how an appendSeparator between them interacts with this suppression, since the separator logic depends on whether the preceding field actually printed anything.

That elseif branch only triggers when iUseBefore is false, so with years before true it's skipped entirely—no separator printed. That matches the expectation that both fields zero means only months prints "0" with no separator, so print(period) should equal "0".

Now checking the second test case with printZeroRarelyFirst on years/months, where I expect years to print "0" instead and months to be suppressed—tracing through the field type and index logic for years to confirm this behavior.

For years with no earlier field to defer to, the loop condition fails immediately so it falls through and prints "0" directly, matching the rule that the first field gets zero when nothing precedes it. For months, the loop finds years is supported and formatted, returning MAX_VALUE to suppress months and defer to years, so years ends up printing "0" while months stays silent—giving the same single "0" output as before, though I still need to differentiate this from the RARELY_LAST case.

To actually distinguish RARELY_FIRST from RARELY_LAST I need three fields—years, months, weeks—all zero, since with only two fields both behaviors produce an identical "0" string. With RARELY_LAST, only weeks should print "0" while years and months get suppressed along with their separators, yielding just "0" overall; with RARELY_FIRST, only years should print "0" instead. But since all three fields use the same bare "0" literal with no distinguishing text, I realize I need to add unique suffixes like "Y" and "M" per field to actually tell which one fired.

I'm constructing a formatter that appends years with suffix "Y", a separator, months with suffix "M", a separator, and weeks with suffix "W", explicitly setting the zero-printing behavior for clarity in the test, then building a Period with all fields set to zero to feed through it.

I plan to verify the RARELY_LAST formatter prints "0W" and a corresponding RARELY_FIRST version prints "0Y" on the same all-zero period, which nicely exercises the branch logic around zero checks and field formatter matching. I also want to add a test for printZeroIfSupported using a formatter with only years and months appended.

For printZeroAlways with appendYears, zero value gets suppressed unconditionally while nonzero prints normally. For printZeroAlways with months on a type that doesn't support months, since type=null bypasses the isSupported check, period.get() returns 0 for unsupported fields per Joda-Time's documented behavior, meaning it would still print zero even without actual support.

I'm planning a test using PeriodType.standard().withMonthsRemoved() to verify this prints "0" as expected, then moving on to thoroughly test the parsing branch next.

For the rejectSignedValues case, I'm checking that calling rejectSignedValues before appendYears means a leading '-' isn't treated as a valid sign, so attempting to parse "-5" should immediately break the parsing loop and cause parsePeriod to throw an IllegalArgumentException.

Now considering maximumParsedDigits(2) with appendYears: parsing "12345" would only consume the first two digits "12" as years, leaving "345" unconsumed. Since parsePeriod likely requires the entire string to be consumed, that leftover text would probably cause a failure, though I'm not entirely certain since that validation logic isn't in the source I'm looking at.

To avoid guessing at behavior outside what I can verify, I realize I can test field formatting directly by calling the parser's parseInto method on the period, text, and position rather than relying on parsePeriod's full-string requirement.

This gives me precise branch coverage for prefix parsing, suffix scanning, mustParse logic, and sign handling.

I want to cover decimal point parsing, maxParsedDigits limits, and parseInt behavior for different digit lengths—avoiding guesses about the unseen PeriodFormatter class by sticking to MutablePeriod, a known standard Joda type.

Now I'm enumerating concrete parseInto test scenarios starting with a basic single-field parser built via appendYears() and toParser().

I'm checking a scenario with a required prefix "P" that's missing from the input—since mustParse is false when printZeroSetting isn't ALWAYS, the prefix parser should fail gracefully by returning a negative encoded position rather than throwing, letting other parsers in the chain try instead.

Next I'm tracing through a case where the prefix succeeds and sets mustParse to true, which then causes the suffix pre-scan to be skipped since that scan only runs when mustParse is still false; this means the digit-parsing limit falls back to the simpler min(maxDigits, remaining length) calculation rather than bounding by a detected suffix position.

I also want to verify the always-force case: when iPrintZeroSetting is PRINT_ZERO_ALWAYS and there's no prefix, mustParse should be set to true right from the start, so parsing an empty string should immediately fail and return the bitwise complement of the position.

Then I'm checking the opposite scenario: a suffix is configured but printZero defaults to RARELY_LAST, so mustParse stays false initially, and if the suffix scan doesn't find a match, the method should gracefully return the complement of the suffix position rather than throwing.

Working through the bitwise complement: ~(-1) equals 0, so the code effectively returns the original starting position when no match was found and mustParse is false, allowing the parser to gracefully move on without consuming input.

For case (f), suffix scan finds "Y" at position1, setting mustParse true, so the limit computed from suffixPos works out to 1, matching the single digit "5" parsed before the suffix. Everything lines up: position advances to 1 after the digit, then to 2 after consuming the suffix, with years set to 5 as expected.

Now I want to test a case where digits exist but the suffix lands at a position that doesn't match the computed digit length.

So with text "5.9Y" and field type YEARS, the digit-parsing loop stops at length 1 (just "5") since '.' isn't accepted, but the suffix scanner skips past '.' and finds "Y" at position 3 — creating the mismatch (0+1≠3), which correctly makes the parser return position 0, deferring to another field. That confirms the graceful-failure branch works as intended.

Tracing the suffix scan character by character: the scanner checks each position for a region match against "Y" first, then falls back to the skip-set of allowed characters ('5', '.', '9') until it hits the actual "Y" at position 3, confirming suffixPos=3. Since a suffix was found, mustParse gets set true, and the digit limit becomes min(10, 3)=3, meaning the digit parsing region is bounded by this suffix position.

But then I realize the digit loop still breaks early at the decimal point since the field type isn't seconds/millis, so length ends up as 1 regardless of that limit of 3. Checking the final condition - suffixPos is 0+1=1 which doesn't equal 3, so it returns position 0, matching the expected test result.

Now I want to verify SECONDS_MILLIS decimal parsing: for "12.345" it should consume the whole string with seconds=12 and millis=345, plus edge cases for fractional length - "5.1" should give millis=100, "5.12" should give millis=120, and "5.1234" should truncate to 3 digits.

For "5.1234", the fraction after the decimal is "1234", and since the formula takes only the first three digits of that fraction, it parses "123" as the fractional value regardless of the trailing "4". I should trust the code's explicit formula rather than guessing the consumption logic—fractLen determines whether to truncate or round, and here fractLen≥3 means just taking those first three digits directly.

Now I'm tracing through the negative case: "-5.5" with sign handling enabled by default. The loop detects the minus sign followed by a digit, sets negative to true, increments length to account for the sign character, and then continues parsing from the next position where it reads the '5'.

The digit increments the length counter and sets hasDigits true, then the '.' character triggers the fraction branch: it records fractPos as the position right after the decimal point and expands the limit by one, since the code only increments length once at the bottom of the loop regardless of which branch executed.

Tracing through "-5.5" step by step: the sign character sets negative true and advances length, then the '5' digit increments length again, the '.' sets fractPos and bumps the limit, and the final '5' is parsed as a normal digit extending the fraction part -- confirming that the whole-number substring length equals fractPos minus position minus one.

The limit is effectively bounded by the remaining string length of 4, so the loop terminates once length reaches 4 since there's nothing left to expand into.

Now parsing the whole number portion: the first two characters "-5" become wholeValue=-5 via parseInt. The fractional length is 1 (since fractLen=0+4-3), so fractValue comes from parsing "5" at fractPos, giving 5, then scaled by *100 to 500, and negated to -500 since wholeValue was negative.

Given this confirms seconds=-5, millis=-500 for "-5.5" with appendSecondsWithMillis(), I should verify sign-handling in the main parse loop only applies when signed values aren't rejected, which defaults to allowed. Given time constraints, I'll cover a reasonable subset of these parseInto branches — fractLen>=3, fractLen==1, fractLen==2, negative sign, missing fraction, and no-digits cases — rather than exhaustively testing every nested variant.

I also want to test the long-digit parsing branch using a 10-digit number with maximumParsedDigits≥10, and verify isSupported() behavior indirectly: appendMonths() with mustParse false and a PeriodType lacking months should skip gracefully and leave the parse position unchanged. I'll construct a MutablePeriod using PeriodType.standard().withMonthsRemoved() to set this up.

Given the complexity, I'm settling on a moderately sized but tractable set of roughly 35 tests, focused on builder-level public API branches plus solid coverage of FieldFormatter.parseInto branches.

Since those access patterns show up directly in the source via internal calls on PeriodFormatter objects, they're accessible at least at package level, and since my test class lives in `org.joda.time.format` too, that's sufficient even if not fully public.

I'll go ahead and use package org.joda.time.format for the test class, then set up the needed imports for JUnit, Period, MutablePeriod, PeriodType, DurationFieldType, and Locale.

Now I'm drafting the list of test methods to cover: clearing builder state, literal appending with null checks, and various combinations of printer/parser arguments being null or valid.

I'm continuing to enumerate test cases for prefix and suffix handling, orphan prefix exceptions, minimum digit padding, and the many separator append variants including adjacent separator errors, field-after conditions, and final text variants.
